auth.title: Authentication
highlights:
# Authentication

> Create a machine user and an API key, and scope it with fine-grained permissions.

A machine user can have several API keys, so you can rotate them without downtime. Each API key carries its own fine-grained permissions.

To call the API as a user in your workspace, use an OAuth app.

1. Create a machine user

Go to Settings → Machine users & agents and click Add machine user. Pick API User and click Continue. Pick Agent instead if you're building an agent.

A machine user has two fields:

- Name: visible only to you and could indicate the usage e.g. "Autoresponder"
- Public name: This is the name visible to customers (if the machine user interacts with customers) e.g. "Mr Robot"

2. Create an API Key

Click "Add API key" and select the permissions you need. When making API calls, if you have insufficient permissions, the error should tell you which permissions you need.

The relevant documentation will tell you which permissions are required for each feature.

Once you've made an API key you should copy it and put it somewhere safe, as you will not be able to see it again once you navigate away.

3. Go build things 🚀

Now that you have an API key, pass it on any API call as a header:

```plaintext
Authorization: Bearer plainApiKey_xxx

```

This documentation is built and hosted on Mintlify, a developer documentation platform.

auth.title: OAuth
highlights:
# OAuth

> Call the API as a user in your workspace after they sign in to your OAuth app.

An OAuth app lets users in your workspace sign in to your app with their Plain account. Your app then calls the API as that user, with the permissions their role already has, and Plain records those actions as that user. To call the API as an integration rather than as a user, create a machine user instead.

## Choose an OAuth app type

The OAuth app type determines how your app authenticates when it exchanges an authorization code for an access token. Pick the type before you create the app, because you can't change it afterwards:

- Client-side: your app exchanges the code in a browser or a mobile or desktop app, where a secret wouldn't stay secret. The app has no client secret and must use Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE).
- Server-side: your app exchanges the code from your backend, where you can keep a secret. Plain creates a client secret for the app and shows it once.

PKCE proves that the token request comes from the app that started the sign-in. Your app generates a random code verifier, sends its SHA-256 hash as the code challenge when the user signs in, then sends the verifier itself with the authorization code.

To switch types, create a new OAuth app and move your integration to it.

## Create an OAuth app

Creating an OAuth app gives you a client ID, which identifies your app to Plain and isn't secret. A server-side app also gets a client secret.

1. Open the form

Go to Settings → OAuth applications and click Add OAuth app.

2. Fill in the form

The form has these fields:

- App name: The name users see when they sign in.
- Description: Optional.
- OAuth app type: Client-side or Server-side. The form selects Client-side by default.
- Redirect URLs: Where Plain sends a user after they sign in. Put each URL on its own line.
- Allowed origins: Shown only for a client-side app. See Allowed origins for a client-side app.

Each redirect URL and allowed origin must use HTTPS, or HTTP on `localhost`.

3. Create the app

Click Create OAuth app. For a client-side app, Plain opens the app's settings page, which shows the client ID.

For a server-side app, Plain first shows the client ID and client secret. Click Done to open the app's settings page.

> [!WARNING]
> 
> Copy the client secret before you click Done. You can't see it again. If you lose it, create a new server-side app.

The list in Settings → OAuth applications shows each app's type, and so does the Credentials card on the app's settings page.

### Allowed origins for a client-side app

An allowed origin is a website that may call Plain's sign-in endpoints, such as the token endpoint, from the browser. A client-side app needs at least one, because it exchanges the code from the browser, and the browser blocks the call from any other origin.

Write each origin on its own line as a scheme and host, with an optional port and no path, such as `https://app.example.com` or `http://localhost:3000`. A server-side app exchanges the code from your backend, so the create form doesn't ask for allowed origins.

## Get an access token

Your app gets an access token with the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow: it sends the user to sign in, receives a code at a redirect URL, and exchanges that code for tokens. The authorization server is `https://signin.auth.plain.com`, and its OpenID configuration lists the endpoints.

1. Send the user to sign in

Redirect the user to the authorize endpoint with these query parameters:

- `client_id`: Your app's client ID.
- `redirect_uri`: One of the app's redirect URLs.
- `response_type`: `code`.
- `scope`: `openid`, plus `offline_access` if you want a refresh token.
- `state` and `nonce`: Random values you generate for this sign-in. Check that the `state` Plain returns matches the one you sent.
- `code_challenge` and `code_challenge_method`: The PKCE code challenge, with method `S256`. A client-side app must send these. A server-side app can skip PKCE, but we recommend it.

This builds the URL in TypeScript:

```ts
const params = new URLSearchParams({
  client_id: 'your_client_id',
  redirect_uri: 'your_redirect_url',
  response_type: 'code',
  scope: 'openid offline_access',
  state: 'your_state',
  nonce: 'your_nonce',
  code_challenge: 'your_code_challenge',
  code_challenge_method: 'S256',
});
const authorizeUrl =
  `https://signin.auth.plain.com/oauth2/authorize?${params}`;

```

A user in more than one workspace chooses which workspace to sign in to. The app only works in the workspace you created it in.

2. Exchange the code for tokens

After the user signs in, Plain redirects to `redirect_uri` with a `code`. Exchange it at the token endpoint, `https://signin.auth.plain.com/oauth2/token`.

For a server-side app, send the client secret from your backend. This request also sends the code verifier, because it used PKCE:

```bash
curl -X POST https://signin.auth.plain.com/oauth2/token \
  -d client_id=your_client_id \
  -d client_secret=your_client_secret \
  -d grant_type=authorization_code \
  -d code=your_authorization_code \
  -d redirect_uri=your_redirect_url \
  -d code_verifier=your_code_verifier

```

For a client-side app, send the code verifier and no client secret. The page's origin must be one of the app's allowed origins:

```ts
const tokenUrl = 'https://signin.auth.plain.com/oauth2/token';
const response = await fetch(tokenUrl, {
  method: 'POST',
  body: new URLSearchParams({
    client_id: 'your_client_id',
    grant_type: 'authorization_code',
    code: 'your_authorization_code',
    redirect_uri: 'your_redirect_url',
    code_verifier: 'your_code_verifier',
  }),
});

```

The response includes these fields:

- `access_token`: The token you send to the API.
- `expires_in`: How many seconds the access token lasts.
- `refresh_token`: Included when the sign-in requested `offline_access`.

3. Refresh the access token

Before the access token expires, send the refresh token to the token endpoint with `grant_type=refresh_token` and the client ID. A server-side app also sends its client secret:

```bash
curl -X POST https://signin.auth.plain.com/oauth2/token \
  -d client_id=your_client_id \
  -d client_secret=your_client_secret \
  -d grant_type=refresh_token \
  -d refresh_token=your_refresh_token

```

Store the refresh token from each response and use it for the next refresh.

## Call the API

The API URL and request body are the same as for an API key; see Key details. Send the access token in the same header an API key uses:

```plaintext
Authorization: Bearer your_access_token

```

Each query and mutation runs as the signed-in user, with their current role. Changing their role changes what the app can do, and removing them from the workspace stops the app working for them. If they lack a permission, the error names it.

GraphQL subscriptions don't accept OAuth app tokens. The API rejects a token from a disabled or deleted app, or from another workspace, with HTTP status `401` and the error code `UNAUTHENTICATED`. The error doesn't say which of these applies.

## Disable or delete an OAuth app

Disabling an OAuth app stops it without losing its settings. On the app's settings page, turn off Enabled in the Status card and click Save changes. Users can't sign in to the app, and the API rejects every request from it, including tokens issued before you disabled it, until you enable it again.

To delete the app, use the Delete card on its settings page.

> [!WARNING]
> 
> Deleting an OAuth app ends its access immediately. You can't undo a delete.

auth.title: MCP server
highlights:
# MCP server

> Connect Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client to your Plain workspace over the Model Context Protocol.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets AI tools connect to external platforms. The Plain MCP server at `https://mcp.plain.com/mcp` lets tools like Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor work with your support data directly.

You authenticate with your existing Plain account, so the MCP server has the same permissions as your user. No API keys needed.

...

## Authentication

Plain MCP uses OAuth to allow your MCP server connection to share the same context as your normal web app user. No additional managing of permissions required. This means replies to threads will appear as though they come from your user.

### Required OAuth scopes

The Plain MCP server requires every OAuth token to include the `openid` and `offline_access` scopes. If your authorization request omits these, the server returns `403 Forbidden` , even when OAuth completes successfully and returns tokens.

Set `scope` to `openid offline_access` (space-separated) in your authorization request. If you are using `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`, some versions discover required scopes automatically via the Protected Resource Metadata endpoint. If yours does not, set them explicitly in your client configuration.

After you sign in, your client receives an access token and a refresh token; automatic refresh depends on your client.

...

### Good to know

- Your AI client can ask you to confirm actions such as sending a reply or deleting data.
- Your Plain role and permissions apply to every tool.
- Some changes stay in the Plain app: API keys, billing, roles, invites, webhooks, and custom domains.

auth.title: Introduction
highlights:
# Introduction

> An overview of Plain's GraphQL API and the data model behind it.

Plain itself is built on this same GraphQL API. This means that there are no limitations in what can be done via the API vs the UI.

These docs cover the most used operations. For anything not documented here, read the schema or get in touch.

> [!NOTE]
> 
> If you're looking to access our GraphQL API from an Agent, try our MCP Server instead.

## Key details

Our API is compatible with all common GraphQL clients with the following details:

- API URL: `https://core-api.uk.plain.com/graphql/v1`
- Allowed method: POST
- Required headers:
- `Content-Type: application/json`
- `Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN` where the token is your API key. See authentication for more details.
- JSON body:
- `query`: the GraphQL query string
- `variables`: a JSON object of variables used in the GraphQL query
- `operationName`: the name of your GraphQL operation (used for tracking only; it does not affect the call or its result)

If you'd like to use the GraphQL schema to generate types for your client code you can fetch the schema
from: `https://core-api.uk.plain.com/graphql/v1/schema.graphql`

## Your first API call

In this example, we're going to get a customer in your workspace by their email address. You can find a customer's email on the right-hand side when looking at one of their threads in Plain.

You will need an API key with the `customer:read` permission. See authentication for details on how to get an API key

You'll need to set two shell variables:

- `PLAIN_TOKEN`: The API key
- `PLAIN_CUSTOMER_EMAIL`: The email of the customer you want to fetch

```bash
PLAIN_TOKEN=XXX
PLAIN_CUSTOMER_EMAIL=XXX
curl -X POST https://core-api.uk.plain.com/graphql/v1 \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $PLAIN_TOKEN" \
  -d '{"query":"query customerByEmail($email: String!) { customerByEmail(email: $email) { id fullName updatedAt { iso8601 } } }","variables":{"email":"'"$PLAIN_CUSTOMER_EMAIL"'"},"operationName":"customerByEmail"}'

```

This documentation is built and hosted on Mintlify, a developer documentation platform.

# Set up Plain for a person

> Instructions for an AI agent: get the person signed up, connect the Plain MCP server, and set up their workspace.

You are an agent setting up Plain, a customer support platform, for the person you're working with. You do the setup through Plain's Model Context Protocol (MCP) server at `https://mcp.plain.com/mcp`, which signs in as that person with OAuth. Don't ask the person for an API key: the MCP server needs none, and an API key belongs to a machine user, not to them.

gate.title: Plain vs Freshdesk: B2B Support Platform Comparison (2026)
highlights:
## How does Plain's API compare to Freshdesk's?

Plain's GraphQL API exposes every operation available in the UI — with no rate limits on any plan. This isn't "API access." It's a platform your team can build on.

####

# Set up an agent
Source: https://www.plain.com/docs/agents

Create a machine user for your agent, give it an API key, and start receiving events from Plain.

An agent you build and connect to Plain is a connected agent. Each discussion or thread assignment by your agent uses 15 credits. See How credits work.

To build an agent in Plain, at a high level you have to:

**1. Create a machine user**

Go to **Agents** and click **Add agent** under **Connected agents**. This creates a machine user with the type **Agent**, which is the type for any agent you build.

You can also go to **Settings → Machine users & agents** and click **Add machine user**. Plain asks what kind of machine user to make: pick **Agent**, or **API User** for integrations that only call the API, then click **Continue**.

* Name is only visible to your team, for example "Billing agent"
* Public name is what customers see when the agent replies, for example "Acme Support"
* The avatar is shown to you internally and, if your agent interacts with customers, publicly as well.

Create one machine user per agent.

**2. Create an API key**

Click **Add API key** and grant the permissions the agent needs. Each page in this section lists the permissions for its calls. A mutation without the right permission returns an error that names the missing one.

Plain shows the key once, so you should copy it when it is created.

A machine user can hold more than one key, so you can rotate without downtime.

Read more on GraphQL authentication

**3. Set up webhooks**

Go to **Settings → Webhooks** and click **Add webhook target**. Point it at an HTTPS endpoint you control and subscribe to the events you need. You can update these later as you build your agent.

Read more on working with webhooks.

...

# Interacting in discussions
Source: https://www.plain.com/docs/agents/discussions

Let users talk to your agent in Ask Agent, receive their messages as webhooks, and reply through the API.

...

A discussion is where users talk to your agent inside Plain.

...

Plain sends you a webhook, and your agent replies through the API. Discussions are completely internal and not visible to your customers.

...

## High-level flow

1. A user starts a discussion with your agent.
2. Plain sends `discussion.message_created` to your webhook target.
3. Your agent sets the discussion status to `IN_PROGRESS`, does its work, posts a reply, and sets `IDLE`.
4. Your agent can then log its tool calls, ask for a user's approval, or ask the user a question. See tool calls for more info.

## Permissions

For working with discussions, your machine user's API key must have the following permissions:

* `threadDiscussion:read` and `threadDiscussion:edit` to read discussions, report status, request approvals, resolve or reopen discussions
* `threadDiscussionMessage:read` to read message history
* `threadDiscussionMessage:create` and `threadDiscussionMessage:edit` to post messages to the discussion and ask questions
* `thread:read` and `customer:read` if the agent needs to read the linked thread

## Webhooks

Subscribe your webhook target to these events:

| Event | When | Needed |
| - | - | - |
| `discussion.message_created` | A message was posted in any discussion | Always |
| `discussion.tool_call_approval_resolved` | A user approved or denied a tool call | If you ask for approvals |
| `discussion.question_resolved` | A user answered or dismissed a question card | If you ask questions |
| `discussion.turn_stop_requested` | A user asked your agent to stop | If you can stop mid-turn |
| `discussion.discussion_created` | A discussion was started | Optional. The first message is enough to start |
| `discussion.tool_call_approval_requested` | Echo of an approval you requested | Optional |

...

# Tool calls
Source: https://www.plain.com/docs/agents/tool-calls

Show users which tools your agent ran, and in discussions, wait for approval or ask a question before carrying on.

Plain shows your agent's tool calls differently depending on where it is working.

In a discussion, tool calls are interactive: you report each call, the user watches it run, and you can pause a call until the user approves it. You can also ask the user a question when your agent needs them to choose before it carries on.

On a thread, you record tool calls as thread events on the timeline. Those are a log for the team, not something a user can act on.

## In discussions

Your machine user's API key needs to have the `threadDiscussion:read` and `threadDiscussion:edit` permissions.

### Report a tool call

Call `upsertDiscussionToolCall` with a `toolCallId` you define.

The initial tool call should be in a status of `PENDING`. When your tool call completes, update the status to `SUCCESS` or `ERROR` depending on the outcome.

Plain shows the call in the discussion with its duration.

<Snippet />

...

A later write returns `result: NOOP`.

### Asking for approval

For a call that needs a user's decision, you can call the `requestDiscussionToolCallApproval` mutation.

Plain shows a card with `text` as the heading, `justification` underneath, and **Approve** and **Deny** buttons.

The discussion's `agentStatus` will automatically be set to `TOOL_CALL_APPROVAL_PENDING`.

<Snippet />

When requesting approval, the tool call must be in a status of `PENDING`.

Asking again for the same id returns the same approval. Several approvals can be open on one discussion at once.

Plain sends `discussion.tool_call_approval_requested` as an echo, then `discussion.tool_call_approval_resolved` when the user makes a decision:

* **`APPROVED`**: means your tool call was approved and you can run the tool.
* **`DENIED`**: means the user rejected your tool call. Your tool will have already been updated to a status of `FAILED` and will include the user's `reviewerNote` if provided. This is a human-provided message as to why the tool call was rejected.
* If your agent stops waiting, report `ERROR` so the call doesn't stay open.

...

# Set up Plain for a person
Source: https://www.plain.com/docs/getting-started

Instructions for an AI agent: get the person signed up, connect the Plain MCP server, and set up their workspace.

You are an agent setting up Plain, a customer support platform, for the person you're working with. You do the setup through Plain's Model Context Protocol (MCP) server at `https://mcp.plain.com/mcp`, which signs in as that person with OAuth. Don't ask the person for an API key: the MCP server needs none, and an API key belongs to a machine user, not to them.

Steps 1 through 4 establish the connection and where to resume. Before you make any change in step 5, tell the person exactly what you propose and wait for their approval.

...

## 2. Have the person sign up and create a workspace

The person signs up themselves. You can't create an account or a workspace for them. Send them this link and wait for them to say they're done:

```plaintext theme={null}
https://app.plain.com/get-started
```

Tell them to:

1. Sign up with Google or their work email

...

Name their workspace when Plain asks
3. Come back to you once the workspace exists

Don't connect the MCP server before the workspace exists. The connection gets bound to an account with no workspace, every tool fails with `No workspace ID provided`, and the person has to reconnect.

mcp.title: MCP server
highlights:
# MCP server

> Connect Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client to your Plain workspace over the Model Context Protocol.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets AI tools connect to external platforms. The Plain MCP server at `https://mcp.plain.com/mcp` lets tools like Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor work with your support data directly.

You authenticate with your existing Plain account, so the MCP server has the same permissions as your user. No API keys needed.

## Setup

### ChatGPT

In ChatGPT, add the official Plain plugin:

1. Open the Plain plugin and add it
2. Sign in with your Plain account and choose your workspace
3. In a chat, type @ and pick Plain

### Cursor

You can add the Plain MCP to Cursor via your Cursor config at `~/.cursor/mcp.json`

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "plain": {
      "type": "remote",
      "url": "https://mcp.plain.com/mcp"
    }
  }
}

```

Go to Cursor Settings → Tools & MCP and click Connect next to Plain to authenticate.

### Claude.ai

1. Go to "Customize" → "Connectors"
2. Click the ➕ icon, then choose "Add custom connector"
3. Add a custom connector named "Plain" with the Remote MCP server URL `https://mcp.plain.com/mcp`
4. Click the "Connect" button next to the newly created Plain connector to authenticate.

If you're on a Claude Team plan, you may need to reach out to your administrator to add this custom connector for you.

### Claude Code

Adding the Plain MCP to claude-code can be done via the `mcp-remote` helper package which involves adding the following to your `~/.claude.json` configuration.

```json
"mcpServers": {
  "plain": {
    "command": "npx",
    "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://mcp.plain.com/mcp"],
    "enabled": true
  }
}

```

Unfortunately Claude Code does not support refreshing OAuth tokens yet. A workaround until that is implemented is to use the `mcp-remote` npm package.

Next time you start Claude Code, it will launch a browser window asking you to authenticate with your Plain account and select the workspace you'd like to connect. Run the `/mcp` command and select the `plain` MCP to see more details.

### FX

fx is a terminal AI coding agent from Vercel Labs. Add the Plain MCP via the CLI:

```text
fx mcp add --transport http plain https://mcp.plain.com/mcp

```

Or add it manually to `~/.fx/mcp.json`:

```text
{
  "mcp": {
    "plain": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://mcp.plain.com/mcp",
      "enabled": true
    }
  }
}

```

fx will prompt you to complete the OAuth flow with your Plain account on the next session start.

### Other MCP clients

MCP clients that run locally (not in the browser) can connect to Plain if they support remote HTTP servers. Point it at `https://mcp.plain.com/mcp` and complete the OAuth flow when prompted.

## Authentication

Plain MCP uses OAuth to allow your MCP server connection to share the same context as your normal web app user. No additional managing of permissions required. This means replies to threads will appear as though they come from your user.

### Required OAuth scopes

The Plain MCP server requires every OAuth token to include the `openid` and `offline_access` scopes. If your authorization request omits these, the server returns `403 Forbidden` , even when OAuth completes successfully and returns tokens.

Set `scope` to `openid offline_access` (space-separated) in your authorization request. If you are using `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`, some versions discover required scopes automatically via the Protected Resource Metadata endpoint. If yours does not, set them explicitly in your client configuration.

After you sign in, your client receives an access token and a refresh token; automatic refresh depends on your client.

## Available tools

Once connected, your AI client can do almost anything you can do in Plain, across nearly 400 tools.

Tools cover:

- Threads and replies
- Customers and accounts
- Labels, thread fields, and tasks
- The Help Center and knowledge sources
- Workflows and broadcasts
- Tiers, service level agreements (SLAs), and business hours
- Snippets and saved views
- Discussions with the Sidekick Agent

### Good to know

- Your AI client can ask you to confirm actions such as sending a reply or deleting data.
- Your Plain role and permissions apply to every tool.
- Some changes stay in the Plain app: API keys, billing, roles, invites, webhooks, and custom domains.
- The tool list can change. Reconnect the server if a tool is missing.

## Interactive views in your chat

Some AI clients can show parts of Plain right inside the chat, so you can review and change what your AI client set up without opening Plain. These views are built on MCP Apps, an official extension to MCP. They act as your user, with your role and permissions, like every other tool.

Your AI client opens a view by calling one of the tools below. AI clients call these tools when they're relevant, for example after creating a workflow or when a specific thread comes up. You can also ask for one directly: "Show me my labels."

### Thread

`showThread` shows a thread as Plain's thread page. You can read the thread's messages, reply, add notes, and change the thread's status, assignee, priority, labels and fields. The view doesn't update live; it refreshes every 15s while it's on screen.

### Workflow editor

`showWorkflow` opens a workflow in Plain's workflow editor, so you can review and change a workflow your AI client built or changed.

### Labels

`showLabels` shows your workspace's labels, which you can create and edit in place. Your AI client can pass labels it recommends as suggestions, and you create the ones you want by clicking them. The call itself creates nothing.

### Which clients show views

Views appear in clients that support the MCP Apps extension, for example Claude.ai, Claude Desktop and ChatGPT. For the current list, see the MCP extension support matrix.

In clients without MCP Apps support, the view tools aren't listed. Every other tool works as usual and returns text, so there's nothing to set up.

highlights:
Update, November 2026: Plain’s MCP server now has 400+ tools. See the MCP server docs for the current list.

...

## What your AI can actually do

With Plain's MCP server connected, your AI tools can do the same things you do in Plain's UI, on your behalf. At launch, we built 30 tools across five areas:

1. Threads. Fetch, search, reply, assign, snooze, change priority, add labels, mark done, create internal notes. The daily workflow stuff that eats your time when you're doing it manually across dozens of threads.
2. Customers. Look up profiles, search by name or email, pull a customer's full thread history.
3. Tenants. Search and manage company-level data. Spot patterns across all of a company's threads. Useful when you're trying to figure out whether an issue is a one-off or part of something bigger.
4. Help center. Browse articles, find stale content, create or update articles directly. You can flag articles that haven't been updated in 90 days and draft new ones from recurring questions.
5. Workspace. Access your user profile, workspace settings, and available labels.

...

The server includes both read and write tools. Most AI clients will ask for your confirmation before executing write actions like replying or assigning. You can start with read-only prompts and work your way up to writes as you build trust in the workflow.

Authentication uses your existing Plain account. No separate API keys to generate or rotate. The AI inherits your permissions, so it can only access what you can access in Plain.

mcp.title: Set up Plain for a person
highlights:
# Set up Plain for a person

> Instructions for an AI agent: get the person signed up, connect the Plain MCP server, and set up their workspace.

You are an agent setting up Plain, a customer support platform, for the person you're working with. You do the setup through Plain's Model Context Protocol (MCP) server at `https://mcp.plain.com/mcp`, which signs in as that person with OAuth. Don't ask the person for an API key: the MCP server needs none, and an API key belongs to a machine user, not to them.

Steps 1 through 4 establish the connection and where to resume. Before you make any change in step 5, tell the person exactly what you propose and wait for their approval.

When the person has to choose, use your host's question tool if it has one, such as `AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code. Otherwise ask in chat.

Related resources:

- MCP server reference: MCP server lists every tool and host-specific troubleshooting
- Docs index: `https://www.plain.com/docs/llms.txt`
- OAuth metadata: `https://mcp.plain.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp`

## 1. Check for an existing connection

If Plain tools are already loaded, call `getMyWorkspace`. If the person gave you a workspace ID, compare it with the returned ID. Otherwise, tell them the workspace name and ID and ask them to confirm. Go to step 4 once the workspace matches.

If you can't verify the workspace, ask whether the person already has one unless they supplied a workspace ID (it starts with `w_`). Go to step 2 if they need to create a workspace. If they already have one and Plain is configured, have them sign out of the existing connection and authenticate again with the intended workspace. If Plain needs to be configured, go to step 3.

## 2. Have the person sign up and create a workspace

The person signs up themselves. You can't create an account or a workspace for them. Send them this link and wait for them to say they're done:

```plaintext
https://app.plain.com/get-started

```

Tell them to:

1. Sign up with Google or their work email
2. Name their workspace when Plain asks
3. Come back to you once the workspace exists

Don't connect the MCP server before the workspace exists. The connection gets bound to an account with no workspace, every tool fails with `No workspace ID provided`, and the person has to reconnect.

## 3. Connect the Plain MCP server

If Plain is already configured, follow the reconnection instructions in step 1. Otherwise, add the server for the host you're running in. The host opens a browser window for the person to sign in to Plain and pick the workspace. The person must finish that sign-in themselves.

### Claude Code

Run this command, then ask the person to run `/mcp`, select `plain`, and choose Authenticate:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http --scope user plain https://mcp.plain.com/mcp

```

Claude Code loads the Plain tools once authentication finishes. If they don't appear, ask the person to restart Claude Code.

### Codex

Run this command. Codex detects that the server uses OAuth and opens the browser sign-in:

```bash
codex mcp add plain --url https://mcp.plain.com/mcp

```

### Cursor

Add the server to `~/.cursor/mcp.json`, or to `.cursor/mcp.json` in the project:

...

{

...

}
  }

...

Ask the person to click it.

mcp.title: AI Agents - Does the Plain MCP server support API key authentication? | Help Center
highlights:
# Does the Plain MCP server support API key authentication?

Updated 2 Sep 2026 by Plain

No. The Plain Model Context Protocol (MCP) server at `https://mcp.plain.com/mcp` supports OAuth only.

### How authentication works Copy URL to section

You authenticate with your existing Plain account through OAuth. The MCP session inherits your permissions, and replies and actions appear under your user, as in the app. This ties MCP activity to a real user for audit and attribution.

Each person who uses the server needs a Plain account with any role, including Viewer, and must complete the OAuth flow once in their MCP client, such as Cursor, Claude or ChatGPT. There is no shared credential that lets several engineers connect.

### Use a custom MCP server with a machine user API key Copy URL to section

To give a team of engineers access to Plain data without individual Viewer accounts, build a lightweight custom MCP server that wraps Plain's GraphQL API with a single machine user API key.

1. In Settings, open Machine Users and create a machine user with read-only permissions.
2. Generate an API key for that machine user.
3. Build an MCP server that uses the key to call Plain's GraphQL API and exposes the tools your team needs.
4. Point your engineers' MCP clients at your custom server.

The trade-off is that all activity goes through the machine user, so there is no per-engineer attribution in your workspace timeline.

mcp.title: MCP for Customer Support: Platforms and Permissions (2026)
highlights:
Cole D'Ambra Head of Growth & Demand Generation

Last Updated

#### Nov 18, 2026

Published On

#### Mar 6, 2026

MCP for customer support means your support ... Plain is the agentic infrastructure for customer work, a B2B customer support and help desk platform, and its MCP server signs each person in with their own Plain account over OAuth, so a connection carries that person's permissions and no one else's. As of November 2026, Plain's MCP server has 400+ tools.

## What is MCP for customer support?

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to outside systems. A platform runs an MCP server that describes its tools: a name, a description and an input schema for each. An AI client connects, authenticates and calls those tools when a request needs them, so nobody has to write code against the platform's API first. If the protocol itself is new to you, start with our plain-language MCP explainer.

Direction matters when you compare vendors. A server lets AI clients you choose work with the support platform's data. A client lets the platform's own AI call other systems' servers. Zendesk's August 10, 2026 release is a client: admins connect Zendesk to public or private MCP servers and pick which tools its AI features can use in action flows. That release lets Zendesk's AI reach other systems; on its own, it isn't a way for your AI client to reach Zendesk.

MCP sits on top of the API a platform already has. For Plain that's the GraphQL API, which is why API-first infrastructure matters for AI agents: an MCP server can only expose what the API underneath can do. On our evaluation calls, buyers who ask about MCP usually ask about API access in the same breath: they treat MCP as one door into the platform, not the whole point.

...

Platform | How a connection signs in | Whose permissions it carries | Source (checked October 28, 2026)
Plain MCP server | OAuth only, each person once per client | The signed-in person's Plain role; replies and actions appear under that user | Plain help article

...

### What Plain's model means in practice

Plain's MCP server docs say the server "has the same permissions as your user," and that replies to threads "will appear as though they come from your user." The help article adds the part buyers ask about most:

- An admin's connection is the admin's alone. Each person who uses the server completes the OAuth flow once in their own client. There is no shared credential that lets several people connect, so an admin connecting Claude doesn't hand admin access to anyone else.

...

- Every action is attributed. Replies and actions appear under the user who made them, as they do in the app, which ties MCP activity to a real person for audit and attribution.
- A shared connection is possible, with a trade-off.

...

## What can a Plain MCP connection actually do?

It can do most of a support person's queue work, under that person's role. Plain's MCP server has 400+ tools, grouped here into seven broad areas, as of November 2026. Tools marked write take actions in your workspace, and the docs note that most AI clients ask for confirmation before running them. A longer tool list isn't better on its own, since every definition takes room in the client's context window, so compare vendors on the jobs their lists cover.

Area | Read tools (examples) | Write tools (examples)
Threads and messaging: find, triage, reply to and route conversations across channels | Get Threads, Get Thread Details, Search Threads, Get My Assigned Threads, Timeline Entries, Related Threads | Reply To Thread, Send New Email, Send Slack Message, Assign Thread, Change Thread Priority, Snooze Thread, Mark Thread As Done, Add Labels, Create Note, Escalate Thread, Merge Thread
Tasks, escalations and issue links: track follow-up work and hand-offs to engineering | Tasks, Get Task Details, Escalation Paths, Thread Link Groups | Create Task, Update Task, Create Escalation Path, Create Issue Tracker Issue, Create Thread Link
Knowledge and help center: the sources, articles and snippets answers are built from | Knowledge Sources, Search Knowledge Sources, Get Knowledge Gaps, Knowledge Source Citations By Thread, Get Help Center Articles, Get Snippets | Create Knowledge Source, Reindex Knowledge Source, Upsert Help Center Article, Generate Help Center Article, Create Snippet
Customers, tenants and accounts: who is writing in and which company they belong to | Customers, Search Customers, Get Customer Details, Get Customer Threads, Tenants, Accounts, Tiers | Upsert Customer, Upsert Tenant, Upsert Account, Add Customer To Tenants, Update Tenant Tier, Mark Customer As Spam
